description: The thesis that contributors earn their value by directing agents rather than doing the work themselves. Worth noticing that this cuts against the flattening argument in the AI & the Person in the Middle pack: if every contributor is now delegating, specifying, reviewing and deciding when to intervene, then management stops being a layer to remove and becomes the general skill - and the middle manager is the one person who already learned it, badly and slowly, on real people. Ask these of managers and of the senior contributors living it.

questions.text: If your contributors are now directing agents, they are doing a version of your job. What do you know about delegation that they are about to learn the hard way?
questions.lands_because: The bridge between the two halves of the subject, and it casts the manager as the person who already holds the scarce skill rather than the person being automated. Guests light up at it.
followups: What did that cost you to learn?
Is anyone teaching them, or are they just finding out?

questions.text: What did you learn in your first year of managing people that transfers to this, and what does not transfer at all?
questions.lands_because: The two-part structure prevents a glib answer in either direction. The non-transferable half is the more interesting one - motivation, growth, and loyalty have no analogue, and naming that clarifies what management actually was.
followups: So what is management, if you take the people part out?

questions.text: How many things can one person actually supervise at once? Have you found the ceiling?
questions.lands_because: Span of control is a real, old, well-understood management constraint that nobody has re-derived for agents. Asking for the ceiling invites a number and a story about hitting it.
followups: What happens to the quality at the top of that range?
Did you notice the ceiling before or after something went wrong?

setting_text.entrepreneur: How many things can you actually supervise at once? Have you found the ceiling?

questions.text: What does a good instruction look like now? Could you teach it to someone?
questions.lands_because: Specifying precisely what you want has become load-bearing, and it is exactly the skill good managers already have. The teachability half tests whether the guest can articulate it or only do it.
followups: What do people get wrong on their first try?
Is it the same skill as briefing a junior?

questions.text: When do you check the work, and when do you accept it? How did you calibrate that?
questions.lands_because: Trust calibration is the whole craft of supervision, human or otherwise. Asking how they calibrated forces a real account rather than a principle.
followups: What did it take to stop checking everything?

setting_text.entrepreneur: When do you check the work and when do you accept it? How did you calibrate that?

questions.text: Who on your team is excellent at the craft and bad at directing it? What happens to that person?
questions.lands_because: The human cost of the shift, made specific. It is the question a manager has been privately worrying about, and asking it plainly usually produces the most honest moment in the conversation.
followups: Is that a training problem or a temperament one?
Do you owe them a path, or does the organization?
questions.avoid_if: The guest is currently running a performance process on someone who fits that description.

questions.text: Delegation feels slower before it feels faster. How do you get someone through that valley?
questions.lands_because: Names the specific reason people abandon delegation and revert to doing it themselves. Managers know this valley intimately from experience and can describe crossing it.
followups: How long is the valley, honestly?

questions.text: Are you hiring for craft or for direction?
questions.lands_because: Seven words that force a real position, and hiring is where a stated philosophy meets an actual decision. The answer tells you what the guest truly believes about the thesis.
followups: Has your interview changed? What do you ask now?
Can you assess direction in an interview at all?

questions.text: How do you tell the difference between someone who directed the work well and someone who got lucky with a good tool?
questions.lands_because: The evaluation problem stated precisely. It is unsolved in most organizations, and a manager improvising an answer live is genuinely interesting listening.
followups: Does your performance process have any idea how to handle that?

questions.text: An agent cannot be held accountable. Where does that leave the person who directed it?
questions.lands_because: Accountability cannot be delegated downward to something that cannot hold it, which means it concentrates on the human director. Most organizations have not said this out loud.
followups: Is that fair, if they could not have caught the error?

setting_text.entrepreneur: An agent cannot be held accountable. Where does that leave you?

questions.text: What is the work you would never hand to an agent? Is that a judgment or a preference?
questions.lands_because: The second clause is the question. It asks the guest to examine whether their line is reasoned or protective, and the good ones will concede they are not sure.
followups: Has that line moved in the last year? Which direction?

questions.text: Does the individual contributor ladder still mean anything?
questions.lands_because: The IC track was built as an alternative to management for people who wanted to keep doing the work. If directing agents is now the work, the premise of that ladder is in question.
followups: What do you tell someone who took that track deliberately?

questions.text: What happens to someone who refuses to work this way and is still genuinely very good?
questions.lands_because: The 'still very good' clause removes the easy answer. It forces the guest to say whether excellence at the craft is now sufficient, which is the question their whole team is quietly asking.
followups: Have you had that person? What did you do?

questions.text: If everyone becomes a manager, what is left that is distinctly yours?
questions.lands_because: Turns the thesis back on the guest. It is the direct answer to the flattening anxiety - either they can name what remains theirs, or the hesitation itself is the story.
followups: Is that a comfortable answer or an uncomfortable one?
questions.avoid_if: Ask it late. Cold, it reads as a challenge to their job security rather than a real question.

questions.text: What should someone entering the workforce now learn first - the craft, or how to direct it?
questions.lands_because: A closer that makes the guest commit. It also connects back to the apprenticeship question - you cannot direct work you have never learned to judge, and most guests will say so.
followups: Can you actually direct work you have never done yourself?

setting_text.entrepreneur: What should someone starting out now learn first - the craft, or how to direct it?
